query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the configurational disorder within the near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst—by deliberately engineering a high‐entropy spinel oxide surface—will simultaneously enhance low‐temperature oxidation activity, resistance to poisoning (from H2O and NO), and long‐term durability without increasing platinum‐group metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with a standard ordered or moderately disordered structure.
generation.intervention: Modify the synthesis process to boost the configurational disorder, transforming the catalyst’s active layer into a high-entropy spinel oxide structure (e.g., by incorporating additional earth-abundant transition metals or adjusting metal ratios during formation).
generation.conditions: Automotive exhaust conditions including transient, low-temperature operation (<150 °C) and exposure to typical pollutants such as water vapor and NO; accelerated aging protocols simulating vehicle lifetime mileage are applied.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced configurational (atomic) disorder in the catalyst’s spinel oxide lattice, leading to an optimized distribution of metal cations and surface oxygen vacancies.
generation.mechanism: The increased disorder promotes synergistic interactions among diverse active sites, which boosts catalytic activity at lower temperatures and improves poisoning-resistance by stabilizing active sites against blocking species. It also retards deactivation mechanisms (e.g., sintering or phase separation) during long-term operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the intervention is expected to yield a lower T10 (temperature for 10% CO oxidation), improved performance under water and NO poisoning, and reduced activity loss over extended operation, thereby meeting stricter emissions standards.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (activity, poisoning-resistance, and durability) of the unmodified near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst under similar automotive exhaust conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected under standard automotive conditions and conventional transient and low-temperature scenarios. Extreme conditions beyond the tested exhaust compositions or unusually high pollutant levels may not benefit from the intervention.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether a single intervention focused solely on increasing configurational disorder can marshal all the necessary improvements simultaneously without unforeseen trade-offs or new deactivation pathways emerging during long-term vehicle operation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of catalysts: one using the standard synthesis for the near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst (baseline) and one employing the modified synthesis targetting high configurational disorder to form a high-entropy spinel oxide surface. Test both catalysts in a lab-scale reactor under simulated automotive exhaust conditions, including transient low-temperature operation (<150 °C), repeated cycles of water vapor and NO exposure, and accelerated aging protocols mimicking mileage degradation.
measurements: Temperature required to achieve 10% CO oxidation (T10 value)
Percentage decrease in catalytic activity over 14 hours of operation
Resistance to performance loss in the presence of H2O and NO
Structural analysis (XPS, STEM) verifying increased disorder in the modified catalyst
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy (increased configurational disorder) catalyst does not exhibit statistically significant improvements—such as a reduction in T10 value and lower activity degradation (by at least 10% relative improvement) compared to the baseline under the same exhaust and aging conditions—the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractEnhancing the activity and stability of earth‐abundant, heterogeneous catalysts remains a key challenge, requiring new materials design strategies to replace platinum‐group metals. Herein, it is demonstrated that increasing the configurational disorder of spinel metal oxides (M3O4, where M is a combination of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) leads to significant improvements in carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation performance. A substantial 63% decrease in the T10 value (temperature to reach 10% CO oxidation) is observed by systematically increasing the number of first‐row transition metals within the spinel oxide. Long‐term stability studies reveal that the most disordered 7‐metal spinel oxide exhibited superior resistance to catalyst deactivation compared to the 4‐metal variant, showing a decrease in activity of only 4.7% versus 12.2% during 14 h of operation. A solventless thermolysis approach is developed to synthesize a series of medium entropy spinel oxide (MESO) and high entropy spinel oxides (HESOs) from discrete, air‐stable molecular precursors.
